title: How to Build a Leadership Pipeline
subtitle: A practical guide to building a church leadership pipeline, identifying potential leaders, and raising them up so your ministry multiplies instead of running on empty.

sections.title: Every Church Is One Resignation From a Crisis
sections.body:
Picture the church where three key volunteers leave in the same season, and there is no one to step in, because no one was being raised to step in. The worship leader moves away. The veteran small group host gets sick. The man who has run the men's ministry for a decade finally burns out. And the church discovers, all at once, that it had no bench, that it had been running on a handful of irreplaceable people, and now it is in trouble.

This is the normal condition of most churches, and it is a failure that was years in the making. We fill roles instead of raising leaders. We find a warm body for the vacancy, breathe a sigh of relief, and never ask who will do this when this person cannot. We live perpetually one resignation away from a crisis, and we call it being lean when it is actually being negligent.

Not a luxury for big churches. A necessity for living ones. A leadership pipeline is simply the deliberate practice of always raising up the next leaders before you need them, so that the church is never dependent on a few exhausted saints and never paralyzed when one of them leaves. The church that builds a pipeline grows. The church that does not eventually grinds to a halt, not because it ran out of money or vision, but because it ran out of leaders, and it never noticed it was running out until they were gone.

sections.title: Learn to See the Leaders You Already Have
sections.body:
The leaders your church needs are probably already sitting in your pews, and you are walking past them every week because you do not know what to look for. Identifying potential leaders is the first work of the pipeline, and it is more about discernment than recruitment.

Look for faithfulness before talent. The person who shows up early and stays late, who does the unglamorous thing without being asked, who can be trusted with a small thing, is showing you the most important leadership trait there is. Jesus said the one faithful in little will be trusted with much, and that is a recruiting strategy. Look for the people others already follow, the informal influence that exists with no title attached, because God often gives the gift before the church gives the office. Look for hunger, the person who keeps asking questions, who wants to grow, who is not satisfied to sit. And look past the obvious, because the loud confident person who volunteers for everything is sometimes the leader and sometimes just the loudest, and the quiet faithful one in the back is sometimes the leader and almost always overlooked.

Then do the thing most leaders never do. Go to them. Tell them what you have seen God put in them, and invite them into something more. Most people have never had a leader name their gifts and call them higher, and that single conversation can change the course of a life. The leaders are there. The question is whether anyone is looking, and whether anyone will say the words.

sections.title: Raising a Leader Is Slower Than Filling a Role
sections.body:
Identifying a potential leader is the easy part. Developing one is slow, costly, relational work, and it is the part most churches skip, which is why their pipelines are empty. You cannot raise a leader with a class. You raise one with your life.

Jesus, who could have done anything, chose to spend three years with twelve men, eating with them, traveling with them, letting them watch him work and then sending them to try it themselves and debriefing when they returned. That is the pattern, and it does not scale the way we wish it would, because leadership is caught more than it is taught. It transfers through proximity, through a younger leader watching an older one handle a crisis, a conflict, a temptation, a disappointment, and learning not from the lecture but from the life. Give people real responsibility before they feel ready, because they grow into what they are entrusted with, and protect them when they stumble, because the stumble is part of the curriculum.

This costs you time you would rather spend doing the work yourself, and it costs you the patience of watching someone do badly today what you could do well. But the leader who only does the ministry produces nothing that outlasts him, while the leader who raises other leaders multiplies. The arithmetic is stark. A church that adds leaders grows by addition. A church that raises leaders who raise leaders grows by multiplication, and over a decade those are not the same church at all.

sections.title: Build the Whole Path, Not Just the Top
sections.body:
A pipeline is not a single program. It is a path with stages, a way for a person to move from a first hesitant step of service all the way to significant leadership, with each stage preparing them for the next. Most churches have a top and a bottom and nothing in between, a few senior leaders and a crowd of spectators, and no clear way to travel from one to the other.

The path has rooms. The first is for the brand new servant, the person taking their first small step, handing out bulletins, helping in the nursery, learning that they belong and can contribute. The next is for the proven helper who is ready to take ownership of something small, to lead a team rather than serve on one. The next is for the developing leader ready to lead other leaders, to multiply rather than merely manage. And at the top are those entrusted with the weightiest responsibility of the church. The point is that every stage has a clear next step, so no one gets stuck, and the gifted helper does not stall out as a permanent assistant because no one ever showed him the door upward.

Build that path on purpose and people will walk it. Leave it to chance and they will not, not because they lack desire but because no one ever told them there was a way forward. The pipeline is finished when a new believer can look at your church and see, however dimly, a path from where they are now to leadership someday, and trust that if they take the first step, someone will be there to call them to the second.

sections.title: Entrust to Faithful Men Who Will Teach Others
sections.body:
Paul gave Timothy one sentence that contains the whole theology of a leadership pipeline. What you have heard from me, entrust to faithful men who will be able to teach others also. Count the generations in it. Paul to Timothy, Timothy to faithful men, faithful men to others, four generations of leaders in a single command, and the whole future of the church riding on whether each generation bothered to raise the next.

This is the work that does not show up on Sunday and changes everything by year ten. It is invisible, slow, and easy to neglect, because nothing breaks immediately when you stop doing it. The church runs fine this month on the leaders you already have. It is five years from now that the cost arrives, when the bench is empty and the faithful few are spent and there is no one coming up behind them, and by then the failure is too old to fix quickly.

I have neglected this. I have been so busy doing the ministry that I forgot to raise the people who would carry it after me, and I have felt the cost when good leaders left and there was no one ready. The leader who builds a pipeline may never see the fruit of it himself, because the harvest comes in a season he will not be there for. That is exactly the point. You are not building something that ends with you. You are entrusting the gospel to faithful people who will entrust it to others, and the measure of your leadership is not the crowd you gathered but the leaders you left behind.
